content.text: Why is the sky blue? Why do objects appear different colours? How do colour TVs work? Understanding colour involves knowing how light interacts with materials and how our eyes perceive different wavelengths. This knowledge is applied in everything from art to television technology to safety signs.
is a mixture of all colours (wavelengths) of visible light.
Sunlight and most artificial light appears white
Can be split into a spectrum using a prism or diffraction grating
The spectrum contains: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV)
is the splitting of white light into its component colours.

content.text: The secondary colours of light are:
They absorb certain wavelengths and reflect others
The reflected wavelengths are what we see
(These are the secondary colours of light!)

The primary colours of light (red, green, blue) combine to make white. This is additive mixing. The primary colours of pigment/filters (cyan, magenta, yellow) combine to make black. This is subtractive mixing.
absorbs some colours and transmits (allows through) others.
A red filter absorbs all colours except red
Objects seen through the filter appear in shades of red or black
When light passes through multiple filters:
Red filter then green filter → No light (all absorbed)
Red filter then yellow filter → Red light (yellow transmits red)
The reflected wavelengths determine the colour we see
The key rule: An object can only reflect colours that are both in the light AND in what it normally reflects.
A red object is viewed under cyan light. What colour does it appear?
Cyan light = green + blue Red object absorbs green and blue, reflects red. But there's no red in cyan light. The object absorbs all the light and appears
What colours does a yellow filter transmit?
Yellow = red + green A yellow filter transmits red and green light, absorbs blue.

When working out what colour an object appears under coloured light, ask: does the object reflect this colour? If not, it appears black. A green object only reflects green light, so under red light it appears black.
White light passes through a cyan filter, then a yellow filter. What colour emerges?
White light through cyan filter: transmits green and blue (absorbs red) Green + blue light through yellow filter: transmits red and green (absorbs blue) Only green is in both transmitted sets.
A blue object is illuminated with yellow light. What colour does it appear?
Yellow light = red + green (no blue) Blue object reflects blue only. No blue in the light to reflect. Object appears

"Red, yellow, blue are the primary colours"
— For light, it's red, green, blue. For pigments, it's cyan, magenta, yellow.
"Mixing all colours of light makes black"
— For light, mixing all colours makes white (additive). For pigments, it makes black (subtractive).
"A red object has red inside it"
— The object has pigments that absorb non-red wavelengths. It reflects red light.
"Blue light through a blue filter is brighter"
— It's the same brightness (assuming perfect filter). Other colours are removed.
— Colour depends on the light source, the object, and the observer. The same object can appear different colours under different lights.

Dispersion separates white light into spectrum (ROYGBIV)

Object colour depends on which wavelengths it reflects

Applications: TVs (RGB), printers (CMYK), stage lighting, photography
— A green object only reflects green light, but red light contains no green, so no light is reflected. (reasoning)
— Magenta = red + blue; a magenta filter absorbs green and transmits red and blue. (filter analysis)

The red filter transmits only red light. The green filter then absorbs red and only transmits green. Since no green light is present after the red filter, nothing passes through the second filter. (sequential filter reasoning)
Yellow reflects red and green but absorbs blue.
Blue light contains no red or green component, so the yellow object absorbs all the blue light and reflects nothing. It appears black. (colour-object interaction)
Each pixel can vary the intensity of its red, green, and blue sub-pixels.

By additive mixing at different brightness levels, the three primary colours of light combine in different proportions to stimulate the three types of cone cell in the eye, creating the perception of millions of different colours. (application of additive mixing)
each colour adds wavelengths, so combining all three primary colours (R+G+B) provides all visible wavelengths, producing white.

each pigment absorbs (removes) certain wavelengths. Cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green, yellow absorbs blue — together they absorb all wavelengths, so no light is reflected and the result is black. (comparison of additive vs subtractive mixing)
